summary: The note argues that systematic risk assessment is essential to planning safe outdoor and environmental education programs. It walks through identifying hazards, evaluating likelihood and severity, developing management strategies, documenting findings, training staff, and building a safety culture. It also covers continuous review, stakeholder involvement, technology tools, and adoption of standards like ISO 31000, citing various experts and dated recommendations.
one_line: Overview of how thorough, ongoing risk assessment underpins safe outdoor education program planning, from hazard identification to culture, technology and standards.
key_facts: The National Council for Outdoor Learning (NCOL) recommended, effective September 10, 2023, that all outdoor educational institutions implement comprehensive risk assessments for every program they conduct.

Emily Thompson, an outdoor education expert with over a decade of experience, recommends brainstorming sessions to list all foreseeable hazards, from wildlife and hazardous terrain to overexertion and improper equipment use.
Safety officer Michael Kendrick said on November 3, 2023 that the next step is to "evaluate the likelihood and severity of these risks."
Laura Vasquez, in a September 25, 2023 workshop, emphasized risk matrices that combine the likelihood of an occurrence with its potential impact to determine a risk level for each hazard.
Evaluation methods include qualitative, semi-quantitative, and quantitative assessments, and historical data on past incidents can show the most common risks for specific activities.
John Markham, a risk management consultant, said in an October 20, 2023 webinar that a three-tier approach of minimizing, monitoring, and planning for all identified risks is most effective.
Risk management measures must be documented in a formal risk assessment report that serves as a guide for staff and is kept as a living document updated with new information.
By December 1, 2023, the Institute for Outdoor Learning (IOL) had mandated that organizations provide comprehensive staff training on risk management protocols and supervision requirements.
Dr. Alex Rivera said at the Outdoor Education Safety Summit on January 11, 2024 that risk assessment is "an ongoing process, not a one-time checklist."
Samantha Doyle, a field education coordinator, noted on February 14, 2024 that program leaders should review the effectiveness of their risk assessments after a program ends.
Principal Kevin Lawrence of Riverside High School advised at a March 3, 2024 town hall that engaging stakeholders in assessment and periodic review ensures diverse input and shared responsibility.
Technology such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for mapping hazards, weather tracking applications, and digital checklists has become integral to modern risk assessment.
ISO 31000 provides widely adopted risk management guidelines across sectors, including education.
